summary: Presents example use cases for DOTS telemetry, which gives a mitigator extra information to fight DDoS attacks more efficiently. It discusses which components are involved, how they cooperate, and what is exchanged.

eli5.summary: When a shop is swamped by a crowd, extra details about who is in it help the guards decide how to handle it.

how does dots telemetry help ddos mitigation
how to use telemetry for automatic ddos response
subtitle: Using detailed attack information to mitigate DDoS attacks more efficiently.

tldr.problem: When a DDoS attack hits a network, operators need to decide quickly which traffic to filter, where to reroute it, and which mitigation system to use. Without detailed information about the attack, these decisions are slow and inefficient, especially during large distributed attacks.
tldr.mechanism: DOTS telemetry extends the base DOTS protocol with detailed metrics about attack traffic: traffic volume percentiles, top talker identities, protocol information, and attack severity. These attributes allow orchestrators to automatically select optimal mitigation resources, redirect traffic through the least congested paths, and adapt mitigation strategies in real time.
tldr.outcome: Networks can respond to DDoS attacks faster and more intelligently, using available mitigation resources efficiently even during massive attacks. Telemetry-driven mitigation enables machine-learning systems to continuously improve attack detection and response.

today: RFC 9387 is an IETF Informational RFC published in 2023. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the primary reference for understanding and implementing DOTS telemetry use cases in DDoS mitigation networks. Implementations continue to adopt DOTS telemetry for automated, intelligent DDoS defense.

sections.title: DOTS Telemetry Overview
sections.content:
DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) is a set of protocols for real-time communication between DDoS detection systems and mitigation systems. The base DOTS protocols, defined in RFC 9132 (Signal Channel) and RFC 8783 (Data Channel), allow a network client to request mitigation and to exchange filtering rules with a mitigation server. These protocols focus on the mechanics of requesting and configuring mitigation.

DOTS telemetry, specified in RFC 9244, enriches the base DOTS protocols with detailed attack metrics. Rather than just saying "mitigate this target", a DOTS client can now say "mitigate this target; we are seeing 900 Mbps of UDP traffic from sources in networks 2001:db8:1::/48 and 2001:db8:2::/48, with the first being the top talker at 100 Mbps". This detailed information allows mitigation systems to respond more intelligently.

RFC 9387 presents practical use cases showing how DOTS telemetry helps. It describes the components involved in each scenario, how they cooperate, and what telemetry attributes are exchanged to achieve efficient mitigation.
sections.eli5: DOTS is the way computers talk about DDoS attacks. DOTS telemetry adds details: instead of just saying "we are under attack", you can say "we are being hit by a flood of traffic from these sources at this rate". That detail helps computers react faster.

sections.title: Network Components and Data Flow
sections.content:
A typical DOTS telemetry deployment involves several components:

Forwarding nodes (routers) observe traffic flowing through the network. They collect statistics using IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export) and send them to flow collectors. During a DDoS attack, these statistics include information about packet rates, bytes, protocol distribution, and source addresses of attack traffic.

Flow collectors aggregate data from forwarding nodes. They process these statistics to identify attack patterns, compute percentiles of traffic volume, and identify "top talkers"—the source networks or addresses sending the most attack traffic. The flow collector acts as a DOTS client, sending this analysis to the orchestrator using the DOTS protocol.

Orchestrators (management systems) receive telemetry from flow collectors and use it to make mitigation decisions. They can query the available capacity of DDoS Mitigation Systems (DMSes) using management protocols like SNMP or YANG/NETCONF. Based on telemetry and DMS capacity, the orchestrator orders forwarding nodes to redirect attack traffic, typically using BGP Flow Specifications (BGP Flowspec) to specify which traffic should be rerouted to which mitigation system. The orchestrator acts as a DOTS server.

DDoS Mitigation Systems (DMSes) are dedicated devices or clusters that filter attack traffic. They have limited capacity and may be shared across multiple customer networks or attack targets. The orchestrator must select which DMS to use based on available capacity and attack volume.
sections.eli5: Routers watch traffic, tell a collector what they see. The collector tells an orchestrator. The orchestrator looks at available DDoS scrubbers and tells the routers where to send the bad traffic. All of this is automatic.

sections.title: Telemetry Attributes and Metrics
sections.content:
DOTS telemetry defines several key attributes that flow collectors can send to orchestrators:

Target prefixes: The IP address prefix (e.g., 2001:db8::1/128 or 192.0.2.3/32) being attacked. Multiple prefixes can be protected in a single mitigation request.

Total attack traffic: Percentile-based metrics of the volume of traffic identified as attack. The metrics include: current-g (the current rate), low-percentile-g (the 25th percentile), mid-percentile-g (the 50th percentile), high-percentile-g (the 75th percentile), and peak-g (the maximum observed rate). Each value is expressed in units such as "megabit-ps" (megabits per second).

Top talkers: A list of source networks or addresses sending large amounts of attack traffic, ranked by volume. For each top talker, the telemetry includes its source prefix and its traffic volume. This allows mitigation to prioritize filtering high-volume sources.

Protocol breakdown: The total attack traffic broken down by protocol (UDP, TCP, ICMP, etc.), allowing mitigation to apply protocol-specific techniques.

Attack severity: A severity level (low, medium, high, critical) assigned to an attack or attack component.

Measurement parameters: The measurement-interval defines the time window over which statistics are computed, and measurement-sample defines the sampling or reporting frequency.
sections.eli5: The telemetry says how much traffic is bad, where it is coming from, what kind of traffic it is, and how serious it is. This helps decide what to do faster.

sections.title: Practical Use Cases
sections.content:
Mitigation of top talkers preferentially: In a large DDoS attack, the DMS has limited capacity. Rather than trying to block all attack traffic, the orchestrator uses telemetry to identify the top-sending networks and redirects only those to the DMS. Forwarding nodes apply BGP Flowspec rules to send traffic from the top talkers through the DMS while less aggressive sources are either allowed through or discarded at the edge. This maximizes the protection of the target with available resources.

DMS selection: A transit provider operates multiple DMSes in different locations. When an attack arrives, the flow collector sends attack volume percentiles to the orchestrator. The orchestrator compares the peak-g metric (the highest observed traffic rate) against the capacity of each DMS and selects the one(s) with sufficient available capacity. This prevents sending traffic to a DMS that is already congested, improving response latency.

Path selection for redirection: The network has multiple paths from the attack target to the DMS. The orchestrator receives telemetry about total traffic volume and attack traffic volume on each link. Using this information, it can select a path that has enough bandwidth to carry the redirected attack traffic without congesting critical links. This keeps normal traffic flowing even while mitigation is active.

Detailed DDoS reports: After an attack, the orchestrator aggregates telemetry data into comprehensive reports showing attack timeline, peak rates, affected targets, and mitigation actions taken. These reports help incident response teams understand what happened and improve future defenses.

Machine learning and adaptation: Flow collectors can apply supervised or unsupervised machine learning to historical telemetry data. Supervised learning uses labeled attack and non-attack traffic to train classifiers. Unsupervised learning (anomaly detection) identifies unusual traffic patterns that might indicate new attack types. The resulting models are deployed in the network to automatically detect and classify attacks in real time.
sections.eli5: Here are ways to use the telemetry: block the biggest attackers first, pick a scrubber that is not busy, use unclogged paths, keep records, and teach computers to spot new kinds of attacks.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Implementing DOTS telemetry requires cooperation among multiple vendors and technologies. The flow collector implements DOTS client software and must export IPFIX data from forwarding nodes. The orchestrator implements the DOTS server and management interfaces (SNMP, YANG/NETCONF) to DMSes and routing systems.

The DOTS specification defines standard JSON structures for telemetry messages. Applications must configure measurement parameters (interval and sample frequency) appropriate for their attack detection and mitigation speed requirements. High-frequency sampling gives rapid response but generates more data; low-frequency sampling reduces overhead but may miss fast-changing attack patterns.

Forwarding nodes must have sufficient capacity to collect and export IPFIX data. For high-speed networks, this can be a bottleneck. Some deployments use sampling (exporting only a fraction of flows) to reduce the load, but this reduces accuracy of the telemetry.

Security of the DOTS protocol itself is critical. The signal channel uses TLS for encryption and authentication. Both DOTS client and server must validate each other's certificates. Telemetry data contains information about network topology and attack patterns, which is sensitive; it should be protected from eavesdropping and modification.
sections.eli5: To use DOTS telemetry, many computers have to work together: the ones watching traffic, the ones collecting, the ones deciding, and the ones scrubbing. All of it is encrypted and signed so only trusted computers can talk to each other.

sections.title: Status and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 9387 is an Informational RFC published by the IETF. It has received IESG approval and represents IETF community consensus on the use cases, even though it does not define a standards-track protocol itself. The RFC does not specify the details of the machine-learning algorithms or the exact DMS selection algorithms; these remain implementation-specific. Instead, it identifies what information flows are needed and what decisions can be made based on telemetry.

The RFC explicitly notes that implementation details like the DMS selection algorithm are out of scope. Different vendors and networks may implement these algorithms differently based on their specific constraints and priorities. The DOTS telemetry specification (RFC 9244) provides the protocol machinery; RFC 9387 explains how to use it effectively.

This RFC is useful for network operators planning DOTS deployments, for vendors implementing DOTS servers and management tools, and for standards bodies defining GOST requirements on DDoS mitigation. It has not been updated or obsoleted and remains the primary reference for DOTS telemetry use cases.
sections.eli5: This document explains use cases and best practices for DOTS telemetry but does not make strict rules. Different networks can do things their own way, as long as they follow the DOTS protocol for talking to each other.
